history.summary: The Brahmayoni Hill Temple stands atop Brahmayoni Hill, the highest hill in Gaya (approx. 24.77027, 84.98345 — hill location, coordinates approximate), reached by a climb of 424 stone steps. The hill is named for a natural fissure said to represent the yoni (female energy) of Brahma; the small hilltop shrine holds a five-headed female image worshipped as Brahmayoni, the creative feminine energy of Brahma. Two caves — Brahmayoni and Maitreyiyoni (Maitreoni) Gufa — and an ancient Ashtabhuja Devi temple also sit on the hill. Buddhist tradition holds that Buddha preached the Fire Sermon here to a thousand former fire-worshipping ascetics, each of whom attained enlightenment. Sources conflict on age: travel sites credit Maratha chieftain Rao Bhau Saheb with the present construction, while one article claims an 11th-century temple destroyed by Aurangzeb in 1633 (UNVERIFIED). Pindas are offered here in large numbers during the Pitripaksha mela.

town_description: Gaya is an ancient city on the Phalgu river in Bihar, one of Hinduism's holiest pilgrimage centres, where pilgrims perform pind daan for ancestors, chiefly at the Vishnupad Temple. It is the gateway to Bodh Gaya, the Buddhist enlightenment site about 15 km away. The city is ringed by sacred hills — Brahmayoni to the south, Ramshila to the north, Pretshila to the northwest — each tied to its layered Hindu-Buddhist heritage.
tradition: Hinduism (Brahma worship; also significant in Buddhist tradition)
